intro: など marks what it follows as one example of a wider set: "X and the like". The spoken forms なんか and なんて keep that "something like X" vagueness, and in speech the vagueness often turns into an attitude: playing something down, brushing it off, or reacting with surprise to it.

skills.rule: Put など after the last example to mean "and so on / such as", then add the particle the whole list needs after など.
skills.explain:
など follows a noun, or the last noun of a list joined with や, and marks it as a sample: 鉛筆やノートなどを買いました "I bought pencils, notebooks and so on". The case particle normally comes after など: などを, などが, などに, などで, などの. を and が never come before it. A single noun with など works too: 週末は掃除などをします "At the weekend I do things like cleaning".

In offers and suggestions など makes the idea sound tentative and polite: お茶などいかがですか "Would you care for some tea, perhaps?" It can also follow a quotation: 「疲れた」などと言っています "He's saying things like 'I'm tired'".

The boundary: など is neutral and fine in writing, and it appears once, at the end. とか is its conversational cousin and goes after every item (AとかBとか). だけ is the opposite: "only these", nothing else.
patterns: N など いかがですか  (polite offer)

examples.jp: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に本[ほん]やペン{など}があります。
examples.en: There are books, pens and other things on the desk.

examples.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]は掃除[そうじ]{など}をします。
examples.en: At the weekend I do things like cleaning.

examples.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みに京都[きょうと]や奈良[なら]{など}へ行[い]きました。
examples.en: In the summer holidays I went to Kyoto, Nara and other places.

examples.jp: テストには漢字[かんじ]や文法[ぶんぽう]{など}の問題[もんだい]が出[で]ます。
examples.en: The test has questions on kanji, grammar and so on.

examples.jp: お茶[ちゃ]{など}いかがですか。
examples.en: Would you care for some tea, perhaps?

contrast.note: とか is casual and normally follows every item: 寿司とかラーメンとか. など is neutral-to-formal and comes once, after the last item.
や goes between nouns (A や B); など closes the list (A や B など). They are partners, not rivals: や joins, など says "and others".
だけ limits: 本だけ "only books". など opens the set: 本など "books and the like".

mistakes.bad: 本[ほん]を{など}買[か]いました。
mistakes.good: 本[ほん]{など}を買[か]いました。
mistakes.note: The case particle goes after など, not before it.

mistakes.bad: 寿司[すし]{など}天[てん]ぷら{など}が好[す]きです。
mistakes.good: 寿司[すし]や天[てん]ぷら{など}が好[す]きです。
mistakes.note: など appears once, at the end; join the earlier items with や. It is とか that repeats.

skills.tip: Can you say "and so on" after the last item? Put など there, then the usual particle after it.

skills.rule: Noun + なんか plays the thing down ("the likes of"); clause or noun + なんて reacts to it with surprise or scorn ("to think that...").
skills.explain:
なんか is the spoken form of など. It can still just give a soft example: お茶なんかどう? "How about tea or something?" But its most typical job is lowering: 私なんか "someone like me" (modesty), 野菜なんか食べたくない "I don't want vegetables or anything like that" (dismissal). It replaces を and が (なんかが is also fine: 私なんかが行っていいの?); other particles stay in front: 東京になんか行かない. It often comes with a negative. Never use it for a person you respect.

なんて marks something as surprising, unbelievable or not worth taking seriously. It follows nouns, and also whole plain-form clauses, where なんか cannot go: 田中さんが先生だなんて知らなかった "I had no idea Tanaka was a teacher"; 一人で山に登るなんて危ない "Climbing a mountain alone? That's dangerous". It also introduces quoted words: 嫌だなんて言わないで.

Keep two look-alikes apart: なんて before an adjective (なんてきれいな花 "what a pretty flower") is the exclamation "what a...", and sentence-initial なんか (なんか変だね) is the filler "kind of". Both are spoken; in writing use など.
patterns: N なんか [negative or dismissive predicate]

examples.jp: 私[わたし]{なんか}まだまだです。
examples.en: Someone like me still has a long way to go.

examples.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]{なんか}したくない。
examples.en: I don't want to do homework or anything like that.
How about some tea or something?

examples.jp: 幽霊[ゆうれい]{なんて}いないよ。
田中[たなか]さんが先生[せんせい]だ{なんて}知[し]らなかった。
examples.en: I had no idea Tanaka was a teacher.

examples.jp: 一人[ひとり]で山[やま]に登[のぼ]る{なんて}危[あぶ]ないよ。
examples.en: Climbing a mountain on your own is dangerous!

contrast.note: など is neutral and fine in writing; なんか and なんて are spoken and usually carry an attitude (modest, dismissive or surprised).
こそ raises a noun to "this one above all"; なんか lowers it to "something like this, hardly worth mentioning".
さえ picks an extreme case, "even X": 名前さえ書けない. なんか and なんて judge X, they do not say how far the claim reaches.

mistakes.bad: 嘘[うそ]をつく{なんか}ひどい。
mistakes.good: 嘘[うそ]をつく{なんて}ひどい。
mistakes.note: After a verb clause use なんて; なんか follows nouns.

mistakes.bad: 宿題[しゅくだい]を{なんか}したくない。
mistakes.good: 宿題[しゅくだい]{なんか}したくない。
mistakes.note: を never comes in front of なんか; drop it.

mistakes.bad: 社長[しゃちょう]{なんか}がいらっしゃいました。
mistakes.good: 社長[しゃちょう]がいらっしゃいました。
mistakes.note: なんか belittles, so it clashes with respect; never use it for someone you honour.

skills.tip: Speaker pulling a noun down? なんか. Rolling their eyes at a whole situation? なんて after the clause. No attitude at all? など.
